Copper-Catalyzed Cyclic Oxytrifluoromethylation of 2,3-Allenoic Acids to
Trifluoromethylated Butenolides
Qiong Yu[a] and Shengming Ma* [a, b]
In recent years, cyclizations
of functionalized allenes have
been developed to be one of
the most efficient methodolo-
gies for the synthesis of cyclic
compounds via intermediacy of
p-allylic metal intermediate
M1 formed by carbometalla-
tion or cycloalkenyl metal in-
termediate M2 formed by the
nucleometalation.
[1] We have
attempted to synthesize b-
methyl butenolides by quench-
ing this cyclic intermediate M2
with iodomethane (methyl
cation). However, the desired
product was not formed and the oxidative dimeric cycliza-
tion of 2,3-allenoic acids was observed unexpectedly,
[2] indi-
cating that the quenching of this type of intermediate M2
with an electrophile is quite challenging. On the other hand,
we reasoned that due to the prevalent high potential biolog-
ical activity of trifluoromethyl substituted compounds
[3] and
butenolides,[4] trifluoromethylation of butenolides will be of
great interest. As a continuation of our research on demon-
strating the new reactivity of functionalized allenes, we pro-
posed to use CF
3
+ ,[5] to trap intermediate M2 with the in-
volvement of higher valent metal catalyst, such as Pd IV.[5a–c, 6]
Herein, we report a copper-catalyzed cyclic oxytrifluoro-
ACHTUNGTRENNUNGmethACHTUNGTRENNUNGylation of 2,3-allenoic acids using a hypervalent tri-
fluoromethyl iodonium reagent, which allows for the synthe-
sis of b-trifluoromethyl
[7] butenolides under mild conditions
[Eq. (3), Scheme 1].
With this notion in mind, we began our studies using
Togni/C29s reagents[8] as the electrophiles. When the reaction
was carried out with 4-phenyl-2,3-butadienoic acid ( 1a ) and
Togni/C29s reagent II in the presence of 10 mol % PdCl 2 in
DMA at 70 8C, no trifluoromethylation product was ob-
served [Eq. (1), Scheme 2]. To our delight, when we switch-
ed the catalyst system to 15 mol % CuCl with 20 mol % 2,2 ’-
bipyridyl ( L1), the reaction proceeded to give the desired
product 2a , albeit in 38 % yield. When Togni/C29s reagent I was
employed, 2a was formed in 17 % yield [Eq. (2), Scheme 2].
To further optimize the reaction conditions, we first tested
other copper complexes, such as CuBr, CuI, CuCl
2,C u -
ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(OAc)2, and [Cu ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(CH3CN)4]PF6 (entries 1–7, Table 1). It is
observed that 1a could be successfully converted to trifluor-
omethylated butenolide ( 2a ) in the presence of a Cu I or
CuII complex. CuBr, an easily accessible and cheap Cu I salt,
gave the best results, affording 2a in 59 % yield. A control
experiment showed that no product was obtained in the ab-
sence of copper complex (entry 12, Table 1). Subsequently,
We investigated the ligand effect by applying a series of bi-
dentate ligands: when we used 1,10-phenanthroline ( L2),
the yield was 52 % (entry 8, T able 1); the use of di-2-pyridyl

were glad to observe that by applying 1,10-phenanthroline-
5,6-dione ( L4) the yield of 2a was further improved to 66 %
(entry 10, Table 1). In the absence of ligand, a significantly
diminished yield was observed (entry 11, Table 1).
To further improve the yield, various solvents were sur-
veyed (Table 2). As summarized in Table 2, the reaction
could proceed smoothly to afford 2a in most of tested sol-
vents except toluene (entry 4, Table 2). We were pleased to
observe that the product 2a in chlorine-containing solvents
gave decent yields (entries 7-10, Table 2), with dichloro-
ACHTUNGTRENNUNGmethACHTUNGTRENNUNGane being the best, affording 2a in 92 % yield
(entry 10, Table 2).
With these optimized conditions in hand, we next ex-
plored the substrate scope of the reaction and found that
various 2,3-allenoic acids can be transformed into desired
products in moderate to good yields (Table 3). When R
1 was
H, a series of substrates with proton, alkyl and phenyl as R 2
may be applied to afford the corresponding products in
moderate to good yields (entries 1–4, 11 and 12, Table 3).
Notably, R
1 could also be proton or electron-donating
groups (entries 5 and 6, Table 3) or electron-withdrawing
groups (entries 7–10, Table 3), giving the desired products in
good yields. Such aryl substituents provide an opportunity

for further synthetic elaboration. It should be noted that
when 4-F or 3,5-(CF 3)2 was employed as R 1 (1h or 1j ), this
trifluoromethylation reaction also proceeded well (entries 8
and 10, Table 3). H, Me and n-C4H9 were all competent sub-
stituent for R 3. The structure of the product was further con-
firmed by X-ray diffraction studies of 2g (Figure 1).[9] When
1.13 g of 1b was used, the corresponding trifluormethylated
butenolide ( 2b ) was obtained in 87 % yield, representing
the robustness of this method (entry 2, Table 3).
To gain insight into the mechanism of this reaction, a radi-
cal scavenger 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-1-piperdinyloxy (TEMPO)
was added under the standard reaction conditions; there
was no trifluoromethylation product 2a formed and radical
coupling TEMPO-CF
3 adduct 3 was formed in 37 % yield
(Scheme 3).
We carried out more experiments to further probe some
details of the proposed mechanisms (Scheme 4). First, we
carried out the reaction with enantioenriched Sa-1k (94 %
ee) under standard conditions. The reaction delivered the
corresponding product 2k in 55 % yield in its racemic form
[Eq. (1), Scheme 4]; furthermore, when 2,3-allenoate 4 was
subjected to the reaction conditions, no desired product was
observed associated with 82 % recovery of 4 [Eq. (2),
Scheme 4], which demonstrates the importance of the
copper carboxylate for the radical addition to allene unit
mediated by its coordination with Cu. In addition, it was ob-
served that when the phenyl group was replaced with n-
hexyl group, no reaction occurred, indicting the importance
of the benzylic stabilization effect for the radical addition
reaction of trifluoromethyl radical.
We may rule out the direct electrophilic trifluoromethyla-
tion of 2,3-allenoic acid ( 1) with Togni/C29s II reagent since no
product was obtained in the absence of copper complex
(entry 12, T able 1). Based on these results, we propose the
possible mechanisms for this reaction. Initially, coordination
of the ligand with CuBr would generate catalytically active
copper species A. The interaction of A with Togni/C29s re-
ACHTUNGTRENNUNGagent II would generate a radical intermediate B, which
would further generate CF
3 radical by releasing (2-iodoben-
zoyloxy)copper(II) bromide ( C). In the presence of 2,3-alle-
noic acid 1, C would generate corresponding coordination
complex D by releasing of 2-iodobenzoic acid, which was
indeed isolated from the reaction mixture as the byproduct.
The coordinated allenyl moiety of intermediate D would be
attacked by trifluoromethyl radical to form the p-allylic
copperACHTUNGTRENNUNG(III) intermediate E,[10, 11] followed by reductive elimi-
nation to release the desired product 2 associated with the
regeneration of the catalytically active Cu I species A
(Path A, Scheme 5). An alternative is the capture of in situ
generated trifluoromethyl radical by the allene moiety of
2,3-allenoic acid 1 producing the corresponding allyl radical
species F. Subsequently, this intermediate would undergo
oxidation with Cu II species C yielding allyl cation G with re-
lease of 2-iodobenzoic acid while regenerating copper(I) cat-
alyst A. G would cyclize to deliver the product through in-
tramolecular attack (Path B, Scheme 5).
In summary, we have developed an efficient copper-cata-
lyzed cyclic oxytrifluoromethylation of 2,3-allenoic acids
under mild conditions, providing a straightforward way to b-
trifluoromethylated butenolides. Due to the potentials of tri-
fluoromethyl substituted butenolides, this method will be of
interest to organic and medicinal chemists. Further studies
in this area including the asymmetric vision of this reaction
with chiral N,N-ligands are ongoing in our laboratory.
